title: Why Fast Internet Still Lags
objective: After this level you can explain the difference between bandwidth and latency, and why distance adds a delay no faster plan removes.
summary: Bandwidth is how much data per second; latency is how long it takes to arrive. Light in fiber needs about 28 ms from New York to London, and no faster plan removes that.

cards.headline: You upgraded to a faster plan. Pages still pause before they load.
cards.body: Internet speed has two separate parts, and a bigger number on your plan improves only one of them. For most websites, the one you're waiting on is the other.

cards.headline: Width and length of the hose

items.label: Bandwidth
points: How much data a connection carries each second
Measured in bits per second, such as Mbps
Like how wide a hose is

items.label: Latency
points: How long data takes to get there
Usually measured as a round trip
Like how long a hose is

cards.headline: Distance you can't buy off
cards.body: Data in fiber travels as light, and glass slows light down: about 4.9 microseconds per kilometer instead of 3.34 in a vacuum. New York to London is about 5,585 km, so light in fiber needs about 28 milliseconds one way and 56 for a round trip. More bandwidth widens the hose. It can't shorten the ocean.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: bandwidth is how much, latency is how long. A faster plan buys the first, not the second.

cards.headline: Why pages feel it
cards.body: Loading a site isn't one trip. The HTML asks for style sheets, scripts and media files, and each request waits for its reply, so the delays add up. That's why engineers say latency, not bandwidth, is the bottleneck for most websites. Their fixes: make fewer round trips, and move the data closer to you.

cards.headline: Speed: split in two
learned: Bandwidth: how much data per second
Latency: how long data takes, often a round trip
New York to London: about 28 ms each way in fiber
Fixes: fewer round trips, data moved closer

questions.prompt: The measure that tells you how much data a connection can carry each second is _____.

options.label: latency
options.rationale: Latency is how long data takes to arrive.

options.label: round-trip time
options.rationale: That's a way of measuring latency.

options.label: a status code
options.rationale: Status codes report how a request went.

questions.explanation: Bandwidth is how much information passes through a connection in a given time, measured in bits per second.

questions.prompt: Match each part of internet speed with what it is compared to.

pairs.right: Like how wide a hose is
Like how long a hose is

questions.explanation: Bandwidth is like how wide a hose is, latency is like how long a hose is, and New York to London is about 5,585 km, a distance light in fiber still has to cross.

questions.prompt: A page needs dozens of separate files. Why does high latency hurt it more than it hurts a single file?

options.label: Each request waits for its own round trip
Bigger pages use up the plan's bandwidth allowance
options.rationale: The problem here is waiting, not capacity.

options.label: Each file makes the light in the fiber slower
options.rationale: Light's speed in glass doesn't change.

options.label: Servers answer only one file per minute
options.rationale: Servers answer quickly; distance adds the wait.

questions.explanation: A page is many requests, and each waits a round trip, so latency adds up; that's why it's the bottleneck for most sites.
